intent: My Amelia City lot is unincorporated Amelia Island and full of live oaks — who has a say over the yard, how close to a tree can the turf base actually be dug, and who supplies the water?
distinctValue: The neighbouring pages hand the reader either a city process (Fernandina Beach's Historic District Council and Certificate of Appropriateness), a gate (Amelia Island's architectural review boards) or a blank (Nassauville's no-HOA parcels). None of them names the one rulebook that governs an Amelia City yard and nowhere else: Nassau County's tree ordinance for the unincorporated areas of Amelia Island, § 37.02, adopted as Ordinance No. 2021-012 on 9 August 2021 and in effect since 7 February 2022. It does not reach the City of Fernandina Beach and it does not reach mainland Nassauville. This page gives the buyer the numbers that set the edge of a turf layout here: protected tree at 5 inches DBH, specimen live oak at 40 inches DBH released only by the Nassau County-Amelia Island Tree Commission, a tree protection zone whose radius is six times the DBH and never less than 72 inches, taken from the controlling code text, § 37.02.N.5.a (the code's own examples: a 50-inch trunk gets a 300-inch radius, an 8-inch trunk the 72-inch minimum; the county's one-page summary's 20-inch / 15-foot example does not follow that formula, which gives 120 inches), and what § 37.02.N.6 and N.7 bar and allow inside that zone: all development activity, including digging, material storage and construction-vehicle parking, is barred, and only utility work, ground covers such as mulch and pine straw laid without machinery, and hand trimming of underbrush are allowed. It also names the water utility the other pages leave vague: the Nassau Amelia system, largely south of A1A, which transferred from Nassau County to the Florida Governmental Utility Authority on 18 September 2025, and which publishes no schedule of its own but points customers at the district and the county.

sources.label: Nassau County Code of Ordinances (Municode): § 37.02, Unincorporated Amelia Island tree protection and replacement
supports: Read 12 September 2026 through Municode's content service for this exact node (api.municode.com/CodesContent, productId 11325, jobId 491936). Node title: "Section 37.02 - Unincorporated Amelia Island tree protection and replacement."
Codification banner for that job: "Codified through Ordinance No. 2026-032, enacted April 27, 2026. (Supp. No. 17)"; posted online 2026-08-27.

§ 37.02.E.1: "A protected tree is any existing, healthy tree as determined by an ISA certified arborist approved by the Board of County Commissioners having a caliper of five (5) inch diameter at breast height (DBH) or greater, and not identified on the most recent Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council Invasive Plant list (Category I or II)."

§ 37.02.E.2: "Specimen trees are any existing healthy live oak as determined by an ISA-certified arborist approved by the Board of County Commissioners, measuring forty (40) inches or more in diameter at breast height, or, a multi-trunk live oak, as determined by an ISA-certified arborist with an aggregate measurement of sixty (60) inches or more in diameter at breast height."
§ 37.02.E.2.a–b: "The exemptions and waivers defined in this article do not apply to specimen trees." "Specimen tree removal shall require a permit from the planning department."

§ 37.02.E.2.d: "The permit request will be considered by the NC-AITC at a public hearing." Criteria: "The tree is dead or has fallen, as determined by an ISA-certified arborist"; "The health and/or structure is sufficiently compromised, and the tree is deemed to have a high likelihood of failure by an ISA-certified arborist with tree risk assessment credentials"; "The application of this section will remove all economically viable use of the property under review"; "The applicant/property owner has demonstrated that no feasible design or development alternative exists that can be implemented that would allow preservation of the specimen tree(s)."
§ 37.02.F: "Tree removal permits, processed through the planning department, are required for the removal of any protected tree, except as outlined in section 32.02.F.1.a below."

§ 37.02.F.1.a (exempt from permit, permit fee and replacement): "Pruning, trimming or removal of trees on residential property that present a danger to persons or property, as determined by documentation from an ISA-certified arborist or a Florida licensed landscape architect."; "Storm-damaged or hazardous trees during and for a one (1) month period following a declared weather state of emergency."; "Minor maintenance activities such as removal of sucker growth, water sprouts, and overhanging branches on mature trees. All work shall be performed in compliance with the best practices as provided by the ISA."; "Fallen trees."

§ 37.02.F.2.b: "Development activity includes, but is not limited to, storage of material or equipment, access roads, haul roads, excavation, grading, deposit of fill material or aggregate, site work, erection of a structure, placement of construction trailers, placement of dumpsters, installation of utilities, operation of heavy equipment, or any other development related activity."

§ 37.02.N.1: "Storage of construction materials or fill dirt is expressly prohibited within the tree protection zone. Protective measures are required to avoid mechanical injuries to roots, trunk, and branches, injuries by chemical poisoning, grade changes, excavations, root compression, and new impervious surfaces."

CONTROLLING ZONE TEXT, § 37.02.N.5.a: "At a minimum, the tree protection zone (TPZ) shall be defined as a circular area around a protected tree with a radius equal to six (6) times the diameter of the trunk of the protected tree at breast height. In no case shall a tree protection zone be less than seventy-two (72) inches. As an example, a protected tree with a DBH of fifty (50) inches will have a tree protection zone with a radius of three hundred (300) inches. A protected tree with a DBH of eight (8) inches will have a tree protection zone of seventy-two (72) inches."

§ 37.02.N.5.b: "Encroachment into the TPZ is allowed only with the written findings from an ISA-certified arborist that such encroachment shall not harm the health of the tree. These findings shall be independently verified by the county's arborist."
§ 37.02.N.5.d: "Trenching or excavation within the tree protection zone of a tree intended for preservation must be done by directional boring/tunneling."

§ 37.02.N.5.e: "A deviation from the minimum size requirements of the tree protection zone may be granted by the NC-AITC if the strict application of this rule will result in the unnecessary destruction of protected trees which can otherwise be preserved through application of best management practices."

§ 37.02.N.6: "All development activities, except those specifically permitted by section 37.02.N.7, shall be prohibited within the tree protection zone, including any construction of buildings, structures, paving surfaces, stormwater retention or detention ponds, and temporary construction activities, including all digging, storage of construction material, mechanical clearing of underbrush and/or parking of construction vehicles."

§ 37.02.N.7 (permitted inside the zone): "Excavating by utility service providers for installation of underground utilities."; "Placement of ground covers such as mulch, pine straw, pine bark, or naturally occurring groundcovers found in the same natural community, and the non-mechanical preparation of the ground surface for such covers."; "Hand trimming of underbrush."

sources.label: Nassau County: Unincorporated Amelia Island Tree Ordinance
supports: "On August 9, 2021, the Nassau County Board of County Commissioners adopted Ordinance No. 2021-012, referred to as the 'Unincorporated Amelia Island Tree Protection and Replacement Ordinance'."
The ordinance's purpose is to "minimize loss of trees to development within the unincorporated areas of Amelia Island".
"Click here for Nassau County Code of Ordinances, Section 37.02 - Unincorporated Amelia Island Tree Protection and Replacement"

Florida Statute, Section 163.045: "A local government may not require a notice, application, approval, permit, fee, or mitigation for the pruning, trimming, or removal of a tree on a residential property if the property owner possesses documentation from an arborist certified by the ISA or a Florida licensed landscape architect that the tree poses an unacceptable risk to persons or property."
NOT ON THIS PAGE: the 7 February 2022 effective date, the 5" and 40" DBH thresholds, and the tree protection zone formula. Those are cited to the ordinance summary PDF instead.

sources.label: Nassau County: Unincorporated Amelia Island Tree Protection Ordinance Summary
supports: "Current tree protection ordinance was adopted August 9, 2021 and went into effect February 7, 2022. The original tree protection ordinance was implemented in 2013."
"Please review 37.02 LDC for further details and a complete list of requirements."
"Protected Tree – Any healthy tree, that's non-invasive , 5" DBH or greater"
"Specimen Tree – Live Oak 40" + DBH or 60" + DBH multi-trunk"
"Removal of a protected tree requires a tree removal permit from the County."

Exemptions: "State law exempts local governments from regulating the removal of any tree that present a danger to persons or property, if documented in a tree risk assessment report from an ISA certified arborist to the property owner."

Exemptions: "Other exemptions: removal of fallen or dead trees, diseased trees as determined by ISA certified arborist; trimming around utility lines; and properly pruning and trimming trees; removal of brush and trees under 5" DBH to reduce overcrowding and improve tree health; and removing trees in emergencies such as storm damage."

Exemptions: "No exemptions for specimen tree removal – requires approval of NC-AITC with the justification that the tree is dead or fallen, or compromised as determined by certified arborist, or keeping the tree would remove all economically viable use of property, or no feasible design alternative exists that would allow for tree retention."
"Permits are not required for pruning/tree maintenance. However, maintenance must be done to ISA and ANSI A300 pruning standards."

SUPERSEDED FOR THE ZONE SIZE — contradicts the controlling code text, § 37.02.N.5.a (Municode source above): "Tree protection zones (TPZ) shall be six times the DBH, or a minimum of 6' – for example, a 10" DBH tree would require a 6-foot protection zone around the trunk. A 20" DBH tree would require a 15-foot protection zone."

ZONE-SCOPED PROHIBITION (this is what the page reports as barred inside the zone): "All development activities shall be prohibited within the tree protection zone, including any construction of buildings, structures, paving surfaces, stormwater retention or detention ponds, and temporary construction activities, including all digging, storage of construction material, mechanical clearing of underbrush and/or parking of construction vehicles."

SEPARATE, NOT ZONE-SCOPED (this is a duty to take protective measures, and the page reports it as such): "Protective measures are required to avoid mechanical injuries to roots, trunk, and branches, injuries by chemical poisoning, grade changes, excavations, root compression, and new impervious surfaces."

SUPERSEDED BY CODE WORDING — the codified § 37.02.N.5.d requires boring for any trenching or excavation in the zone of a kept tree; the county-engineer condition belongs to § 37.02.N.7.a (utility providers): "When trenching or excavation within the tree protection zone of a tree intended for preservation is deemed necessary by the county engineer all trenching and excavating shall be done by directional boring/tunneling."
"Tree barricades shall be installed prior to any development activity occurring on site, other than permitted clearing of brush to access protected trees."

"Residents and developers will need to submit a tree removal application, which includes a tree protection and replacement plan/tree inventory, to the Planning Dept. for review. Applications can be found by visiting the County website or by request via email to treeinfo@nassaucountyfl.com."
"When the request involves removal of three (3) or fewer trees, the inventory/survey does not need to be certified by an ISA-certified arborist, but must contain all requisite information."

"Table 37-4[A] Amelia Island Protected Native Canopy Trees" lists Quercus virginiana (Live Oak), Quercus laurifolia (Laurel Oak), Magnolia grandiflora (Southern Magnolia) and Juniperus silicicola (Southern Red Cedar), among others.

"The NC-AITC is comprised of 5 voting members appointed by the BoCC consisting of one Planning and Zoning Board representative and lay citizens who are residents of the unincorporated area of Amelia Island"

Enforcement names the county arborist: "Violations of this ordinance should be reported to the code enforcement department ... and to the County Arborist at treeinfo@nassaucountyfl.com or 904-530-6300."

The summary's own pointer to the controlling text: "Please review 37.02 LDC for further details and a complete list of requirements." The summary is still cited on the page for the 7 February 2022 effective date and for the county arborist's email address.

notes: The legacy research record for amelia-city-fl flagged the tree question as an open gap: it recorded that Nassau County 'operates an Amelia Island Tree Commission concerned with tree protection on unincorporated Amelia Island — SCOPE UNVERIFIED on the check date (the county's own PDF would not parse); confirm before making claims about tree-removal or root-zone permitting.' The county's own ordinance page and its published ordinance summary close that gap. The summary PDF was downloaded and read locally with pdftotext -layout.

Citation anchoring, corrected 12 September 2026: the county's /1273 web page carries the adoption date, the ordinance number, the unincorporated-Amelia-Island scope, the § 37.02 code reference and the Florida Statute 163.045 hazard-tree exemption, and nothing else. It does NOT carry the 7 February 2022 effective date or any DBH or protection-zone number. Those are now cited on the page to the ordinance summary PDF, which does carry them.

Prohibition scope, corrected 12 September 2026: the summary contains two different sentences and they are not interchangeable. Only one is scoped to the tree protection zone — 'All development activities shall be prohibited within the tree protection zone, including ... all digging, storage of construction material, mechanical clearing of underbrush and/or parking of construction vehicles.' The other is a general duty — 'Protective measures are required to avoid ... grade changes, excavations, root compression, and new impervious surfaces.' The page now reports the zone ban and the protective-measures duty as two separate things rather than merging grade change and root compression into the zone ban.

Removed 12 September 2026: the page previously concluded 'Cutting a base is digging, grade change and compaction by definition, so on a wooded lot the tree circle, not the property line, is what the turf edge gets measured from.' No source establishes that a homeowner's turf install is a 'development activity' under § 37.02 — both prohibition sentences are framed around development and construction. The page now states what the ordinance says, says plainly that the county has not settled in writing whether a residential turf base is development activity or a new impervious surface, and tells the reader to put that question to the county arborist at treeinfo@nassaucountyfl.com with a tree survey before the layout is fixed.

Exemptions added 12 September 2026: the permit requirement was previously stated flat. The summary's own Exemptions section lists dead and fallen trees, diseased trees as determined by an ISA-certified arborist, storm emergencies, utility-line trimming, proper pruning and trimming, and brush and trees under 5" DBH; and the county's web page quotes FS 163.045, which bars local permitting for a residential tree an ISA-certified arborist or Florida licensed landscape architect documents as an unacceptable risk. Both now appear on the page. The specimen-tree line is reported as the county states it — 'No exemptions for specimen tree removal – requires approval of NC-AITC' — with the justifications the summary lists.

Water shortage order, re-anchored 12 September 2026: the page previously cited Action News Jax for 'the Phase III order that took effect on 11 May 2026' covering 'all of Nassau County'. That URL now returns a 451 geo-block and cannot be read, and both parts of the claim were wrong against the district's own pages: SJRWMD published the declaration on 13 May 2026, and the order covers 'Portions of ... Nassau ... counties within the District', not all of it. The page now cites the district's own declaration, its watering-restrictions page for order 2026-017 and the schedule, and its 3 September 2026 update confirming the order remains in effect. The Action News Jax source has been dropped from the page.

The legacy record said water service on the unincorporated south island is 'county/JEA or private/community system rather than the City of Fernandina Beach utility — VERIFY per address'. FGUA's own systems page settles the system identity: the Nassau Amelia water and wastewater system, largely south of A1A, now run by FGUA. It does not prove which utility bills any individual parcel, so the page still tells the reader to read their own bill, and notes that some south-end parcels are on wells.

Still not settled by any source: whether Nassau County treats a residential artificial-turf base as a 'development activity' or a 'new impervious surface' under § 37.02 on a particular lot, and whether the county will accept an arborist's encroachment finding under § 37.02.N.5.b or a Tree Commission deviation under § 37.02.N.5.e for a turf base on a given lot. The page asks the reader to email treeinfo@nassaucountyfl.com with a tree survey and ask those questions, rather than answering them.

The 25 percent mitigation requirement, the tree fund, preservation credits and tree bank exchange areas in the same ordinance were read and deliberately left off the page: they attach to new development, not to a homeowner laying a lawn, and would mislead a buyer.

Zone size RESOLVED 12 September 2026 against the controlling code text. The county's one-page summary says "six times the DBH, or a minimum of 6'" but gives "A 20\" DBH tree would require a 15-foot protection zone"; six times 20 inches is 120 inches, or 10 feet, so the example does not follow the formula. The controlling text is Nassau County Code § 37.02.N.5.a, read on Municode (Supplement 17, codified through Ordinance No. 2026-032 of April 27, 2026) and matched word for word against Ordinance 2021-012 as adopted: the zone is a circle with a radius of six times the DBH, never less than 72 inches, with the code's own examples of a 50-inch DBH at a 300-inch radius and an 8-inch DBH at 72 inches. Unit conversions used on the page: 72 inches = 6 feet; 300 inches = 25 feet; 6 x 20 inches = 120 inches = 10 feet. The page now states the code's rule and examples, cites Municode, and tells the reader the summary's 20-inch / 15-foot example does not match the code.

Protected tree size RESOLVED 12 September 2026: code § 37.02.E.1 and the summary agree on 5 inches DBH; the code adds that the tree must not be on the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council Category I or II invasive list, which the page now says instead of 'non-invasive'. Specimen live oak: 40 inches DBH, or 60 inches aggregate for multi-trunk (§ 37.02.E.2).

Re-anchored to code 12 September 2026 because the summary's paraphrases differ from § 37.02: (1) exemptions — the code's permit exemptions (§ 37.02.F.1.a) are hazard trees on residential property documented by an ISA-certified arborist or Florida licensed landscape architect, nursery stock, storm-damaged or hazardous trees for one month after a declared weather emergency, minor maintenance to ISA best practice, county right-of-way safety work, utility-line maintenance by the utility, and fallen trees; diseased nonresidential trees, thinning and other emergencies (§ 37.02.F.1.b) still need a permit and a notarized arborist letter. The summary's 'dead ... diseased trees' exemption is not how the code reads, so the page's FAQ now lists the code's exemptions. (2) Boring — § 37.02.N.5.d requires boring/tunnelling for any trenching or excavation in a kept tree's zone; the summary had merged in the county-engineer condition that § 37.02.N.7.a attaches to utility providers. (3) The page now reports the § 37.02.N.7 permitted list and the § 37.02.F.2.b development-activity definition (excavation, grading, deposit of fill or aggregate) as the code states them, and still asks the county arborist how they apply to a turf base.
